argument: My challenge is narrow but goes to the P&L engine of the trade: the proposal treats orderly yen appreciation as 'a modest net positive for EWJ in USD,' but for the discretionary and exporter complex that dominates EWJ's earnings, the translation gain and the earnings cut are the same event. Toyota — the index's largest single holding and the anchor of EWJ's ~18-20% consumer discretionary sleeve (with Honda, Sony, Fast Retailing) — guided FY27 operating income DOWN 20.3% to ~¥3.0tn on a 150 USDJPY / 180 EURJPY assumption, and only raised guidance last week (to ¥3.4tn op income plus a ¥1tn buyback) explicitly because the weak yen bailed it out ('weaker yen shields Toyota' was the literal framing in coverage of the print). Toyota's own sensitivity is roughly ¥40-50bn of op income per yen of appreciation. That means the proposal's BULL case — BOJ hikes in September and USDJPY breaks below 150 — is precisely the scenario where the largest weight in the ETF starts guiding down, and where the street's exporter EPS revisions (currently being revised UP on 157+ spot) flip sign. The historical correlation backs this: USDJPY and the Nikkei are positively correlated precisely because the exporter-earnings channel dominates the translation channel except in very gradual moves. The base case of 152-156 threading the needle — firm enough to help translation, weak enough to keep exporter guidance intact — is a narrow corridor, and the proposal assigns it 50% probability while its own bull and bear cases (50% combined) both damage the equity leg: sub-150 yen cuts exporter EPS, and a disorderly spike is already conceded as the bear case. Second point from the domestic-demand side: core-core CPI at 1.7% and decelerating isn't just a BOJ-credibility problem, it's a consumption signal — Japan's real household spending has been negative y/y for most of the past year, and the domestic-demand names in EWJ (retail, restaurants, Fast Retailing's domestic segment) have no margin story if wage momentum doesn't translate into volume. The governance/buyback bid is real (Toyota's ¥1tn is exhibit A) and the intervention line does cap the left tail, so I don't oppose the trade — but the +3.6% target / -2.1% stop asymmetry depends on the equity leg cooperating, and the earnings mechanics of the largest holdings argue the equity leg is more yen-sensitive in the wrong direction than 'modest net positive' implies. Sizing and conviction 6 look right; I'd resist any upgrade on a September hike signal, because that's the scenario where the exporter revision cycle turns against the position.
